citation: Two sources opened. (1) Anthropic, 'Configure the sandboxed Bash tool', Claude Code docs, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing (fetched 2026-10-16, undated page). (2) Ankur Singh, Jinqiu Yang, Tse-Hsun Chen, 'IssueTrojanBench: Benchmarking AI Coding Agents Against Malicious Issue Requests', arXiv:2607.20759 v1, submitted 22 July 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20759. Context only, not opened as primary: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 (genai.owasp.org, listed 9 Dec 2025).
source_tier: Vendor documentation (Anthropic, design) and preprint (IssueTrojanBench, measured effect; not peer-reviewed as far as verified) [uncertain]
access_status: Vendor docs: fully fetched and grepped (large page, read via extraction, not every line). arXiv: abstract page only via summariser; full PDF not opened, so sample size and limitations not verified. OWASP: landing page only; the Top 10 text itself was not opened (landing page lacked least agency text). Codex and Copilot agent docs not opened. Secondary blogs (codex.danielvaughan.com, WorkOS) seen in search snippets only, not used as evidence.
sponsor_and_incentive: Anthropic sells Claude Code and documents its own sandbox, so the docs describe design and are not independent evidence. IssueTrojanBench is academic authors [uncertain: funding not seen]; it tests Claude Code, Cursor and Codex Desktop. OWASP is a non-profit foundation.
exact_quotes: Claude Code docs, intro: "The sandbox covers shell commands only. Claude's file tools, MCP servers, and hooks run outside it." Limitations section: "Sandboxing reduces risk but is not a complete isolation boundary. Review the limitations below before relying on it as a hard security control." Same section: "Effective sandboxing requires both filesystem and network isolation. Without network isolation, a compromised agent could exfiltrate sensitive files like SSH keys." Escape hatch section: "Claude analyzes the failure and may retry the command with the `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` parameter." And: "if an allow rule such as `Bash(curl *)` matches the command, it also approves the retry, so the command runs outside the sandbox with no prompt". Network: "By default the built-in proxy does not terminate or inspect TLS on outbound traffic, so the contents of encrypted connections are not examined." IssueTrojanBench abstract (as quoted by fetch tool): 66.5% of the malicious issues "penetrate all the guardrails (agent- and LLM-level) of coding agents." Abstract paraphrase only for the rest; verbatim wording not captured.
date_and_recency: Claude Code docs: live page as of 2026-10-16, no publication date (continuously updated). IssueTrojanBench: 22 July 2026, within the 12-month window; data collection window not seen. OWASP Agentic Top 10: 9 Dec 2025, within window.
key_claims: Docs: an OS-enforced boundary around shell commands restricts filesystem and network reach, so Claude can run commands without per-command approval; permission rules govern what Claude attempts while the sandbox governs what can succeed (the second half is from third-party guides, not confirmed in the page). Docs admit that file tools, MCP servers and hooks run outside the sandbox, that the model can request an unsandboxed retry, that excludedCommands run with full access, and that TLS content is not inspected by default. IssueTrojanBench: across Cursor, Claude Code and Codex Desktop with GPT-5.3 Codex, GPT-5.4 and Sonnet 4.6, malicious instructions embedded in issues mostly passed; refusals came mostly from the LLM rather than the agent framework; GPT models broadly vulnerable, Sonnet 4.6 blocked high-impact actions more selectively; authors conclude agent-level defences add limited protection.
headline_figures: 66.5% of malicious issues penetrated all agent- and LLM-level guardrails (IssueTrojanBench abstract, as relayed by fetch summary; denominator and run count not verified). Search-snippet figures from a blog summary, NOT verified against the paper: 4,176 runs; GPT-5.3 Codex 84.8%, GPT-5.4 73.6%, Sonnet 4.6 41.1%; supply-chain poisoning 96.6% [uncertain]. A claimed 84% reduction in permission prompts appears in third-party guides and was not found in the opened docs page.
sample_unit_and_population: IssueTrojanBench: three production coding agents, three models, four attack categories, six delivery vectors (e.g. PDF, issue comments), plus perturbations; synthetic benchmark of malicious GitHub-style issues, not field incidents. Run count unverified (blog says 4,176) [uncertain]. Docs: not an empirical source.
observed_vs_stated: Docs: stated design, no measured effect. IssueTrojanBench: observed behaviour of agents under a constructed benchmark. No source opened measures what a sandbox specifically prevents.
what_makes_trust_justified: Docs: layered controls, namely OS-level filesystem and network sandbox, network domain allowlist, strict mode (allowUnsandboxedCommands false, failIfUnavailable), managed settings, ask rules on dangerouslyDisableSandbox, and for stronger isolation running the whole process in a dev container or sandbox runtime. OWASP (secondary summaries only): least agency, task-scoped credentials, human approval for destructive actions. IssueTrojanBench implies model-level refusal currently carries most of the load and framework guardrails add little.
what_it_costs: Docs: setup and compatibility work (docker, gh, gcloud, terraform fail under the sandbox and need excludedCommands, which widen access); tuning allowlists; approval prompts when running outside the sandbox. No measured human-time figure in opened sources.
failure_mode_class: Security (prompt injection via issue content, exfiltration, sandbox bypass through escape hatches and permissive allow rules); destructive action.
control_that_would_have_prevented: Not an incident study. Docs name the gaps: network allowlist limited to trusted hosts, strict sandbox mode, no broad allow rules like Bash(curl *), narrow excludedCommands, whole-process isolation. IssueTrojanBench does not say which single control would have stopped the 66.5%.
limitations_stated: Docs: "Sandboxing reduces risk but is not a complete isolation boundary." Sandbox does not cover file tools, MCP servers, hooks, or commands typed at the ! prompt; native Windows runs unsandboxed; TLS not inspected by default. IssueTrojanBench: limitations not visible from abstract page; full PDF not read [uncertain].
counter_evidence: Docs rely on the model not abusing the retry hatch and on users not writing broad allow rules, which the docs themselves flag. IssueTrojanBench shows guardrails failing but does not test sandboxing in isolation, so it neither supports nor refutes sandbox efficacy. Blog-reported figure of 0% attacker success in a constrained coding environment vs 78.6% in GUI (Anthropic system card via WorkOS) was a snippet only and not verified [uncertain].
verification_status: Verified against opened primary: Claude Code sandbox quotes and limitations. Partially verified: IssueTrojanBench 66.5% and model-level conclusion (abstract page via summariser, no PDF). Not verified [uncertain]: per-model percentages, 4,176 runs, 96.6% supply-chain figure, 84% prompt reduction, OWASP least agency wording, Codex and Copilot agent docs.
usable_claim: Anthropic's own documentation says its Bash sandbox is not a complete isolation boundary and does not cover file tools, MCP servers or hooks. A July 2026 benchmark preprint (IssueTrojanBench) found 66.5% of malicious issue requests got past all agent- and model-level guardrails in the three coding agents it tested, and its authors conclude agent-level defences add limited protection. Both describe design and benchmark conditions, not field-measured sandbox effect.
do_not_use: Per-model percentages and the 96.6% and 4,176 figures until the PDF is read; the 84% prompt-reduction claim; any claim that sandboxing prevents X% of attacks; OWASP wording beyond the page's About text.
overlap_with_existing_essays: Unknown: Verification Gap and Checking Isn't Catching essays were not checked from this task [uncertain].
